title: Clare of Assisi (1194–1253)
hook: she follows Francis into poverty and leads her sisters for forty years

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict and Scholastica: a Rule that opens with listen, and a storm that made a brother stay. Your line was pray and work.

Palm Sunday night, in the hill town of Assisi. A young woman from a noble family waits until the house is asleep. Her family has marriage plans for her. She has other plans. She slips out a side door, through the dark streets, down the hill, to a tiny chapel in the woods where a man named Francis and his barefoot brothers are waiting with torches. There she takes off her fine clothes, puts on a rough tunic, and Francis cuts off her long hair. By morning her family is furious. They come to drag her home.
screen: `PALM SUNDAY NIGHT, ASSISI.` → `OUT THE SIDE DOOR.` → `FRANCIS CUTS HER HAIR.`

segments.voice: Her name was Clare, from the Latin for bright, clear. Her relatives found her in a convent chapel and tried to pull her away. She held on to the altar cloth and showed them her cropped head, and they gave up. Soon her younger sister Agnes ran away to join her too. Francis gave them a home at San Damiano, a small, run-down church just outside town, and there Clare led a community of women, the Poor Ladies, for the rest of her life. Other convents owned land, so the sisters were secure. Clare refused. She fought popes, politely and for years, for what she called the privilege of poverty: the right to own nothing at all, and to trust God and the kindness of the town for bread. Two days before she died, the pope finally approved the rule she had written for her sisters herself. And she wasn't grim about any of it. The people who knew her described her as joyful. Poor and glad. Once, the story goes, soldiers came over the walls of San Damiano. Clare, sick in bed, had the Blessed Sacrament carried to the door and prayed before it, and the soldiers left. Near the end, too ill to get to Mass, she said she could see and hear it on her wall. That's why, in 1958, the Church made her the patron saint of television. Her sisters, the Poor Clares, still pray in monasteries all over the world.
screen: `CLARA: BRIGHT, CLEAR.` · `SAN DAMIANO, FOR LIFE.` · `THE PRIVILEGE OF POVERTY.` · `PATRON SAINT OF TELEVISION.` · then, large: `POOR AND GLAD.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing in your life that's gotten too full, a closet, a calendar, a phone's home screen, a habit of buying, and picture it with less: not empty, just lighter. Clare wasn't trying to be miserable; she was trying to be free. If you pray, you can ask for the gladness she had.
clara. Latin for bright or clear, Clare's own name, who gave up everything to own nothing at all.
Your line: poor and glad. She chose it, and fought popes to keep it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Clare on 11 August, and the Poor Clares, her sisters, live enclosed lives of prayer and poverty in monasteries worldwide.

notes: Palm Sunday night 1212 (some sources 1211) at the Portiuncula; age about 18. Confirm.
The 'side door' is the tradition of the 'door of the dead'; confirm.

Privilege of poverty granted by Innocent III (c. 1216) and confirmed by Gregory IX (1228); Rule approved by Innocent IV on 9 August 1253, two days before her death on 11 August. 'First rule written by a woman approved by a pope' is the common claim; confirm.
Soldiers at San Damiano (1240, Frederick II's troops, often described as Saracen mercenaries): tradition; the script says 'the story goes'. The script avoids naming the soldiers' religion. Confirm.
Patron of television: Pius XII, 1958 (announced 1957/58). Confirm.
About forty years at San Damiano (1212–1253). Confirm.
